In [[commutative algebra]], a [[commutative ring|ring]] <math>R</math> is said to be '''arithmetical''' (or '''arithmetic''') if any of the following equivalent conditions hold:
# The [[localization of a ring|localization]] <math>R_\mathfrak{m}</math> of <math>R</math> at <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> is a [[uniserial ring]] for every [[maximal ideal]] <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> of <math>R</math>.
# For all [[ideal (ring theory)|ideals]] <math>\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{b}</math>, and <math>\mathfrak{c}</math>,
#:<math>\mathfrak{a} \cap (\mathfrak{b} + \mathfrak{c}) = (\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b}) + (\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{c})</math>
# For all ideals <math>\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{b}</math>, and <math>\mathfrak{c}</math>,
#:<math>\mathfrak{a} + (\mathfrak{b} \cap \mathfrak{c}) = (\mathfrak{a} + \mathfrak{b}) \cap (\mathfrak{a} + \mathfrak{c})</math>

The last two conditions both say that the [[lattice (order)|lattice]] of all ideals of <math>R</math> is [[distributive lattice|distributive]].

An arithmetical [[domain (ring theory)|domain]] is the same thing as a [[Prüfer domain]].
